Dinny O’Brien’s/Shaskeen

Great tune, jocklet. I knew it as “Dinny O’Brien’s” hornpipe some years before Pat Kilbride recorded it, and “De Danann” recorded it under that name too. Joe Burke regularly plays it under the name “The Shaskeen”, and it is easy to see the similarities between it and the reel.
P.S. - I put in “D O‘B’s” as an alternative title and it’s come up in about 6 recordings. Those sre more likely to be the reel of that name, and it might avoid confusion if you delete “D.O’B’s” as a title.. Sorry about that. Well done.

Different tune…

The hornpipe posted by “JACKB” above isn’t Paddy Keenan’s “version”of this reel, it’s a completely different tune altogether, which just occasionally happens to have the name “Dinny O‘Brien’s”. The only thing they have in common is “Dinny O’Brien’s” name as a title.

Regarding Kenny’s comment, that hornpipe is in fact a version of the tune (sometimes known as) The Butchers of Bristol and was first recorded from the playing of Jem Byrne on an ediphone cylinder.

Annie’s Favourite, X:11

Most commonly known in Wexford as ‘The Broadway Hornpipe’, but also widely known around the country as ‘The Rover through the Bogs’. There is a Broadway in County Wexford, which may account for the tune’s popularity in County Wexford, although Paddy Taylor apparently played it regularly at The Broadway Pub in Fulham in the 60’s which may account for that title either. It was recorded by the piper Liam Walsh, and later by the piper Tommy Kearney of Waterford as ‘The Butchers of Bristol’, and versions of it with that title are to be found in English mid-19th century manuscripts.

↳ Posted by John E Roche on July 2nd, 2023.

Annie’s Favourite, X:12

Transcribed from the Hennebry wax Cylinder recording of the piper, Jem Byrne playing this as one of two ‘Wexford Hornpipes’. The second is a setting of Pretty Maggie Morrissey, which is often called simply ‘The Wexford Hornpipe’. These are among the earliest known recordings of traditional music, recorded in Ring Co.Waterford c. 1905. I believe Byrne at that time was living in Kilkenny. He was born I think in Athy, but was either one of the Wicklow travelling Byrne pipers, or possibly the Carlow Byrnes mentioned in O‘Neill’s Irish Minstrels and Musicians. Perhaps someone knows which? It’s a most distinctive setting of this tune widely played in County Wexford today as ’The Broadway Hornpipe’.

↳ Posted by John E Roche on August 2nd, 2023.
